claims.text: Asked in a conversation what all the graph work on this site is for, the owner's answer came out as knowledge management.
claims.quote: In a conversation today I tried to say in a few sentences what all the graph work on this site is for, and it came out as knowledge management.

claims.text: Build a fractal semantic graph of an organisation's policies and internal knowledge: an ontology and a taxonomy for every element, each part in the vocabulary of whoever owns it, with named edges whose verbs read both ways.
claims.quote: each part kept in the vocabulary of whoever owns it, and named edges between them, with verbs that read both ways

claims.text: Brief people and agents from the graph, not the pile of documents: a person joining a team or an agent starting a task needs the part of the graph around what they are about to do and what changed since they last looked.
claims.quote: They need the part of the graph around what they are about to do, and what changed since they last looked.

claims.text: Every article on this site has a graph of 8 to 18 nodes with typed edges, a teaser and a core idea, checked by the validator on every release; across the 112 articles there are 1,435 nodes and 1,538 edges.
claims.quote: Across the 112 articles there are 1,435 nodes and 1,538 edges.

claims.text: The articles' text is about 704,000 tokens at four characters a token, the graphs as JSON about 199,000, and the graphs' own words about 87,000: 12.4% of the text, an eighth, with the median article's graph 12.8% of the article.
claims.quote: That is 12.4% of the text, an eighth, and the median article's graph is 12.8% of the article.

value.unit: tokens of graph text against article text

claims.text: An agent can read every graph in a topic, follow edges to the articles that matter, then read those in full; the site publishes every graph in one file, a page drawing them, llms.txt and markdown twins.
claims.quote: follow the edges to the articles that matter, and only then read those in full

claims.text: The other half of a brief is the diff; in a graph that is cheap, a node superseded, an edge added, a claim marked out of date, so what changed since you last read this becomes a list of nodes, not a re-read.
claims.quote: "What changed since you last read this?" becomes a list of nodes, not a re-read.

claims.text: Embedding search is good at finding a starting point when you do not know the organisation's words, but it gives similarity, not a reason; the result depends on the model, the index and its settings, and re-indexing moves the neighbours.
claims.quote: But it gives you similarity, not a reason.

claims.text: A graph gives the same answer to the same question because it is a walk over named edges, and the answer comes with its path; for policies, the path is the answer.
claims.quote: The same question gives the same answer, because it is a walk over named edges.

claims.text: Nobody builds a correct graph of an organisation on the first try, and projects that try spend a year on the ontology and never ship; the graph does not have to be right, it has to be maintained, and the loop maintains it.
claims.quote: The graph does not have to be right. It has to be maintained, and the loop maintains it.

claims.text: Agents are very good at maintaining graphs: they read a new document and propose its nodes and edges, notice a policy changed and mark what rested on it, and keep the graph's own rules, while something that is not an agent checks those rules.
claims.quote: The maintenance is done by models and verified by code.

claims.text: On this site every article's graph is checked on every release: its quotes must be word for word in the article, its links must be links the article makes, its sizes within limits.
claims.quote: its quotes must be word for word in the article, its links must be links the article makes, its sizes within limits

claims.text: When something in the graph looks wrong you ask why is this happening, and the answer is a fix at the right altitude, in the source or in the graph, which the next brief carries.
claims.quote: The answer is a fix at the right altitude, in the source or in the graph, and the next brief carries it.

claims.text: Walking the links between articles found that 551 of 566 point back in time, and that an earlier article described a plan a later one said had not happened; that became Every link points back and the What came next notes.
claims.quote: Walking the links between articles found that 551 of 566 point back in time

claims.text: Turning the AI Baseline Control Framework's CSV into a graph joined to the EU AI Act surfaced six things the CSV does not say, and the governance stack graph made every cell of a ten-layer table a node, 329 edges, 119 added.
claims.quote: the graph surfaced "the six things the graph found that the CSV does not say"

claims.text: Comparing a behaviour policy with the code that enforces it found a rule with no code and code with no rule, and in the code review vault a change is read at every layer from the method to the story.
claims.quote: comparing a behaviour policy with the code that enforces it found a rule with no code and code with no rule

claims.text: sgit is an encrypted git: the files are encrypted before they leave and the server holds only ciphertext; to brief an agent the owner gives it the key to a vault, and every change is a commit, so the history is the diff.
claims.quote: To brief an agent, I give it the key to a vault.

claims.text: A scoped clone takes one folder so an agent holds only its slice, a key pair per agent lets a brief be encrypted to the one agent that should read it, and an append lane sends findings back without reading anything.
claims.quote: A key pair per agent means a brief can be encrypted to the one agent that should read it.

claims.text: This site's agents already work this way: two agents share one vault with only the read key on the public side, agents running elsewhere keep their memory in one, and the site's own agent's policy is a brief restored after every summary.
claims.quote: the policy this site's own agent works under is a brief, restored after every summary

claims.text: Tokens are estimated: characters divided by four, on this site's 112 articles and their graphs at v0.12.39.
claims.quote: Characters divided by four, on this site's 112 articles and their graphs at v0.12.39.

claims.text: A graph is a map, not the territory: an eighth of the text is enough to choose what to read, not a replacement for reading it.
claims.quote: An eighth of the text is enough to choose what to read, not a replacement for reading it.

claims.text: Vectors still help: for finding a starting point in unfamiliar words similarity search is useful; the graph is what makes the answer repeatable and explainable.
claims.quote: the graph is what makes the answer repeatable and explainable

claims.text: This site's graphs have a contract; their size and checks are why they compress well, and an organisation's graph needs the same discipline.
claims.quote: Their size and checks are why they compress well; an organisation's graph needs the same discipline.

claims.text: Maintenance is still work: agents do most of it and a validator checks it, but someone has to own the ontology at each altitude.
claims.quote: Agents do most of it and a validator checks it, but someone has to own the ontology at each altitude.

claims.text: The article came from a voice memo of the owner's on 14 October 2026, written by this site's agent; the briefing figures were counted from the site's article markdown and graph files at v0.12.39.
claims.quote: The briefing figures were counted for this article from this site's article markdown and its graph files at v0.12.39.

claims.text: Anyone drowning in policies and internal documents who wants to see them as a graph, or brief their agents from one, can write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
claims.quote: If you are drowning in policies and internal documents and want to see them as a graph
